Um, rituals? No, I wouldn't say that. I don't have to, like, touch a doorknob a certain number of times or wash my hands over and over or anything. Well, it definitely jumps around. Over this past year, it’s like it started with just worrying about my mother’s safety, with the nightlights and her wandering, but now it’s spread to... everything. Finances, staff decisions at the library, deadlines, the house, whether I'm actually being a good daughter to her... even really small things just feel like they’re about to completely unravel. 

Like the other day, I was looking at the gutters on my house, and they were a little clogged with leaves—we have this enormous oak tree in the front yard, beautiful in the summer, but a total nightmare in the fall. The leaves get absolutely everywhere. Anyway, I started thinking about the gutters, and then suddenly I was convinced the water was going to back up, ruin the roof, leak into the foundation, and I'd be financially ruined and have to sell the house and move my mother into a facility, which she would absolutely hate. 

And speaking of facilities, did you know how much they charge for assisted living these days? I was looking at brochures just... just in case, you know? And the pricing structures are completely opaque. It's like they don't want you to know what you're actually paying for. It reminded me of when we were trying to negotiate the new database subscriptions at work. The vendors give you these bundled packages that include fifty journals you don't need just to get the three you do, and if you try to unbundle them, they charge you double. It's extortion, honestly. The budget committee was furious, but what are we supposed to do? The students need access to the archives. 

But, um... yes, the worry. It definitely jumps from one thing to another. It never just stays on one topic.

We actually just got this huge donation of 16mm films from the local historical society that I've been trying to archive, and they smell strongly of vinegar, which means they're degrading, so I have to keep them separated from the main collection. \n\nBut yeah, no matter how many lists I make or how hard I try to redirect myself, the worry just stays stuck in my head.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever feel like you have to perform specific rituals or actions to reduce your worry?\n\nPatient: Um, rituals? No, I wouldn't say that. I don't have to, like, touch a doorknob a certain number of times or wash my hands over and over or anything. I mean, I do have a very specific way I organize my workspace, but that's just because of my job. Like, my archival pens have to be on the exact left side of my keyboard, always. \n\nSpeaking of which, it is getting so incredibly hard to find good quality acid-free pens these days. The supplier we've used for the last ten years just got bought out by some massive corporate conglomerate, and the ink in the new batches takes just a fraction of a second longer to dry. Which doesn't sound like much to most people, I know, but when you're labeling delicate microfilm sleeves, that fraction of a second is the difference between a perfectly clean label and a massive, permanent smudge. I actually had to throw out an entire box of archival sleeves last Tuesday because of it, and they are not cheap. The budget committee is already breathing down my neck about our department's spending... \n\nBut, um... wait, what were you asking? Oh, right, actions to stop the worry. No, I don't do anything like that. I just sit there and worry.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel a strong need to repeat certain tasks or mental acts to relieve anxiety or worry?\n\nPatient: No, not really. I mean, I don't have to repeat things in my head or do tasks over and over to feel better. I just... I just think about the worries a lot. Like a broken record. Speaking of records, we have this massive collection of vinyl at the library, mostly spoken word and local oral histories from the 1960s, and we're supposed to be digitizing them. But the turntable we have is so finicky, and the needle—the stylus—needs to be replaced, but of course, the model is discontinued. I spent three hours on eBay last night trying to find a replacement part, and I finally found one from a seller in Germany, but the shipping is astronomical. I don't know how I'm going to justify that to the budget committee, especially after the whole pen fiasco. They already think the media department is a money pit. \n\nBut, um... no, I don't do anything repeatedly to make the anxiety go away. I wish I did, honestly. Maybe it would help. I just kind of sit with it and let it run laps in my brain.\n\nDoctor: Is your worry usually about a specific thing or situation, or does it seem to jump around to a lot of different things?\n\nPatient: Well, it definitely jumps around. Over this past year, it’s like it started with just worrying about my mother’s safety, with the nightlights and her wandering, but now it’s spread to... everything. Finances, staff decisions at the library, deadlines, the house, whether I'm actually being a good daughter to her... even really small things just feel like they’re about to completely unravel. \n\nLike the other day, I was looking at the gutters on my house, and they were a little clogged with leaves—we have this enormous oak tree in the front yard, beautiful in the summer, but a total nightmare in the fall. The leaves get absolutely everywhere. Anyway, I started thinking about the gutters, and then suddenly I was convinced the water was going to back up, ruin the roof, leak into the foundation, and I'd be financially ruined and have to sell the house and move my mother into a facility, which she would absolutely hate. \n\nAnd speaking of facilities, did you know how much they charge for assisted living these days? It reminded me of when we were trying to negotiate the new database subscriptions at work. The budget committee was furious, but what are we supposed to do? The students need access to the archives. \n\nBut, um... yes, the worry. It definitely jumps from one thing to another. It never just stays on one topic.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your worrying is interfering with your daily life or work in any significant way?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, I... I think it really is. It’s starting to affect my work, which terrifies me, honestly. I've always been the person who catches everything. But lately, I’ve started missing these small but important details at the library. Like, I mislabeled an entire series of photographs from the 1920s last week because I was so distracted worrying about my mother. \n\nAnd speaking of photographs, we have this incredible collection of glass plate negatives that were donated by a local family, and they are just stunning. The detail you can get on glass plates is something you just don't see with digital photography. But they are so fragile, you have to handle them with these special lint-free gloves, and the humidity in the storage room has to be exactly 40%. I had to call the emergency HVAC guy, and of course, it was a Sunday, so they charged time and a half. The budget committee had an absolute fit about the overtime charge. Concentrate at work? Yes. Oh, absolutely. It's getting so frustrating. Like, during cataloging reviews or staff meetings, I’ll be looking right at the screen or the agenda, and suddenly I realize I haven’t absorbed a single word. My mind has just completely wandered off into some problem I think I should have prevented, or some disaster I need to fix.

The radiator was leaking, of course, because the maintenance guy, Phil, used the wrong sealant on the valve. Phil means well, but he's always trying to cut corners. He told me he learned plumbing from watching YouTube videos, which is just terrifying when you think about the fact that he's responsible for a building full of irreplaceable paper. 

But... wait, concentration. Right. Yeah, it's definitely harder. I just can't seem to keep my focus on what's right in front of me anymore.

They already think the media department is a money pit. \n\nBut, um... no, I don't do anything repeatedly to make the anxiety go away. I wish I did, honestly. Maybe it would help. I just kind of sit with it and let it run laps in my brain.\n\nDoctor: Is your worry usually about a specific thing or situation, or does it seem to jump around to a lot of different things?\n\nPatient: Well, it definitely jumps around. Over this past year, it’s like it started with just worrying about my mother’s safety, with the nightlights and her wandering, but now it’s spread to... everything. Finances, staff decisions at the library, deadlines, the house, whether I'm actually being a good daughter to her... even really small things just feel like they’re about to completely unravel. \n\nLike the other day, I was looking at the gutters on my house, and they were a little clogged with leaves—we have this enormous oak tree in the front yard, beautiful in the summer, but a total nightmare in the fall. The leaves get absolutely everywhere. I was looking at brochures just... just in case, you know? And the pricing structures are completely opaque. It's like they don't want you to know what you're actually paying for. The budget committee was furious, but what are we supposed to do? The students need access to the archives. \n\nBut, um... yes, the worry. It definitely jumps from one thing to another. It never just stays on one topic.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your worrying is interfering with your daily life or work in any significant way?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, I... I think it really is. The detail you can get on glass plates is something you just don't see with digital photography.
